t: A Simple Way To Calm An Excitable Class
q: Excitability is a major cause of misbehavior. Which is why it is present in virtually every classroom where the teacher is struggling.
You see, students take their cue from you. So if you’re stressed and uptight, if you’re flustered and rushing around, it will reflect in their behavior.
It’s to slow down. It’s to begin moving deliberately and gracefully. It’s to smooth out your movements, motions, and actions and downshift to a lower gear.

Those who practice Tai Chi know this phenomenon well. The very act of articulating the elegant movements of this ancient martial art has a unique way of eliminating unwanted energy and restoring emotional equilibrium.
Just ease up on your pace a little and your breathing will deepen, your muscles will soften, and you’ll begin to feel more composed and confident.
But what’s so cool about this technique is that it’s contagious. Your calm presence will spread from one student to the next and fill every corner of your classroom.
It will remove any and all disquieting feelings and usher in contentment, cooperation, and self-awareness.

Classroom excitability is largely a reflection of the teacher's own energy and stress level, since students take their cue from the adult in the room.

Rather than relying on willpower to overcome stress or forcing oneself to feel calmer, he draws a comparison to Tai Chi, where deliberately slower, more graceful movement naturally settles both body and mind.
The technique is inspired by Tai Chi, where deliberate, unhurried movement naturally restores emotional equilibrium.

He explains that this deceleration does not need to be noticeable or dramatic to be effective — easing off the pace slightly deepens breathing and softens muscles, producing composure from the outside in.
A teacher's calm, slowed presence is contagious and spreads through the classroom, settling restlessness in students as well.

t: How To Hold Difficult Students Accountable
q: How should I hold difficult students accountable? It's a topic I haven't covered specifically because the answer is so simple and direct: Just like everyone else.
It’s a way of enforcing consequences with all students without causing friction or resentment.

Because, when a difficult student is in the midst of transitioning into the well-behaved student you envision them to be, it’s a tenuous time. One stern lecture or burst of anger from you could send them in the opposite direction.
Hey Anthony, I really appreciate how well you’ve been doing, but I have to give you a warning for breaking rule number two.
It reinforces their image of you as a leader to be trusted, as a person of integrity they can count on to do what they say they’re going to do.
The student will look down, nod their head, and say, 'I understand.' You may also receive an apology, although it usually comes at the end of the day.
It’s a simple little change, hard to believe it could make much difference. But for those few students on the cusp of great and enduring change . . . It can mean the world to them.

t: How To Bring New Students Into Your Peaceful Classroom ful-classroom/
q: Although often calm and quiet in the beginning, whatever habits and behaviors were permitted at their previous school will eventually bubble to the surface.
Typically, a ten minute conference with the new student is all that is needed to ensure a peaceful transition.
Very simply and directly state that in your classroom students behave, and that will be expected of them as well.
You’ll then make the same promise you make to all of your students that you will follow your classroom management plan to a tee.
This is a critical step in earning their trust and support of you and your program.
If your classroom management is solid, and you’re steadfast in your consistency, even the most difficult new students fall in line without you having to say another word.
They experience the intrinsic allure of a happy and productive classroom. And they want to be part of it too.
